meta.titre: British Consular Rule on the Cameroon Coast: consuls, courts and the missed chance of 1884
meta.sous_theme: British consuls, Courts of Equity and the loss of the coast to Germany
tags: british consular rule on the cameroon coast

sections.contenu_markdown: Before the German flag flew over Douala in 1884, the British were already the main foreign power on the coast of Cameroon. Their representatives were not governors but consuls, officials who watched over trade, fought the slave trade and settled disputes. Examiners ask for the names of the consular officials, the work they did and the events of 1884 in short questions worth one or two marks each. This course gives you the facts and the logic that connects them.

items: A consul is an official who represents his country's interests and its citizens in a foreign place.
Legitimate trade means trade in goods such as palm oil, as opposed to the trade in slaves.
A protectorate is a territory under the protection and partial control of a stronger state.

sections.titre: British consuls on the Cameroon coast before 1884
sections.contenu_markdown:
### Why Britain was on the coast

Britain abolished the slave trade in its empire in 1807 and then used its navy to stop other traders. It wanted to replace the sale of slaves with legitimate trade in palm oil and other goods, and the coast of Cameroon was one place where this trade grew. British merchants and Baptist missionaries lived on the coast and looked to their government for protection.

### The consuls

| Official | Role |
|---|---|
| John Beecroft | First British consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra from 1849, based at first on the island of Fernando Po |
| Later consuls | Dealt with the chiefs, trading disputes, missionaries and the suppression of the slave trade |
| Edward Hewett | Consul in the 1880s, sent in 1884 to make treaties with the Cameroon coastal rulers |

### What the consuls did

- Made treaties with coastal rulers by which the chiefs promised to give up the export of slaves.
- Supported Courts of Equity, where traders and chiefs together settled disputes about debts and trade. They were set up in coastal trading towns, such as Douala.
- Protected British traders and missionaries.
- Supported legitimate trade and the settlement of freed slaves, for instance at Victoria, founded in 1858 by the missionary Alfred Saker.

The consuls had very little real power. Britain did not govern the coast and had no wish to spend money on it. This is called informal control.

### Why Britain lost the coast

Duala kings asked Britain for protection from 1879, but the British government gave no firm answer. In July 1884 the Germans signed a treaty with the Duala kings, and Hewett arrived a few days later (on 19 July), too late to sign. Britain regained a share of Cameroon only after the First World War, when part of it became a British mandate.

variantes.quand_utiliser: When the command word is Name, State or Write down
variantes.contenu_markdown: Give the exact fact. The consul of the 1880s is Edward Hewett. The event that upset his plans in July 1884 was the German treaty with the Duala kings. Two-mark questions need two points, so count the number of marks and give that many facts.

variantes.nom: Describe the work of the consuls
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks what the British did on the coast
variantes.contenu_markdown: Use a list of four points: treaties against the slave trade, Courts of Equity, protection of traders and missionaries, support for legitimate trade. Add one example to each point if you can.

variantes.nom: Why Britain failed to annex the coast
variantes.quand_utiliser: When the question asks about the missed chance in 1884
variantes.contenu_markdown: Write about British slowness: the government gave no firm answer to the petitions, was unwilling to pay for new colonies, and the consul arrived days after the Germans. Contrast this with German speed.

etapes.justification: 'Describe' asks for what the consuls did, not why Britain lost the coast.
etapes.resultat_markdown: Aim: three or four activities, each with an example.

sections.conclusion_markdown: Model answer: British consuls on the Cameroon coast carried out several tasks before 1884. First, they worked to end the slave trade, making treaties with coastal chiefs in which the chiefs promised to stop the export of slaves. John Beecroft, the first consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra, was the first of these officials. Second, the consuls supported Courts of Equity in the coastal trading towns, such as Douala. In these courts traders and chiefs together settled disputes about debts and trade. Third, they protected British traders and missionaries and encouraged legitimate trade in palm oil. However, the consuls had little real power, because Britain did not govern the coast and did not want to spend money on it.

items.erreur_markdown: The British governed the Cameroon coast as a colony before 1884.
items.pourquoi_faux: Britain had only consuls, who had limited powers. The coast was not a British colony.
items.correction_markdown: Write that Britain exercised informal influence through consuls and treaties.

items.erreur_markdown: Confusing the German envoy with the British consul: 'Nachtigal was the British consul sent in 1884.'
items.pourquoi_faux: Gustav Nachtigal was German. The British consul was Edward Hewett.
items.correction_markdown: Match the name to the country: Hewett for Britain, Nachtigal for Germany.

items.erreur_markdown: Writing about the German takeover when the question asks about the work of the British consuls.
items.correction_markdown: Stay on what the consuls did: treaties, courts, protection and trade.

items.erreur_markdown: Saying that Hewett arrived before the Germans and signed the treaty.
items.pourquoi_faux: Hewett arrived on 19 July 1884, a few days after the German treaty, and was too late.
items.correction_markdown: State that Hewett was late and that Germany won the coast.

items.enonce_markdown: State two reasons why Britain placed consuls on the West African coast in the nineteenth century.
items.solution_markdown: Any two of: to end the slave trade; to encourage legitimate trade, such as palm oil; to protect British merchants; to protect missionaries; to make treaties with local rulers. **Two clear reasons** earn both marks.

items.enonce_markdown: Explain what a Court of Equity was and why traders and chiefs needed one.
items.solution_markdown: It was a court in which European traders and local chiefs sat together to settle disputes. They needed it because trade involved credit, and quarrels about debts could damage trade and cause violence. The court gave a peaceful way to settle them. **A joint court for settling trade disputes.**

items.enonce_markdown: Assess the achievements and the failures of British consular rule on the Cameroon coast. [8 marks]
items.solution_markdown: Award marks for achievements: treaties against the slave trade, Courts of Equity, protection of trade and missionaries, support for legitimate trade. Award marks for failures: little real power, no governing structure, reluctance to spend money, the failure to answer the petitions, arrival of Hewett after the Germans, and the loss of the coast. Credit a judgement, for example: **the consuls kept order in trade, but their lack of power and Britain's reluctance cost it the coast.**

items_markdown: Britain came to the coast to end the slave trade, to support legitimate trade and to protect its traders and missionaries.
John Beecroft was the first consul for the Bights of Benin and Biafra; Edward Hewett was the consul of the 1880s.
Courts of Equity were joint courts of traders and chiefs that settled trade disputes.
The consuls had little real power because Britain did not govern the coast.
Hewett arrived on 19 July 1884, after the German treaty with the Duala kings, and was too late.
Britain regained a share of Cameroon only after the First World War, as a mandate.
